facts.l: the range of a cat's purr

story: I'm Mira. My first cat, Fıstık (“pistachio” in Turkish), came into my life when I was five. That little cat taught me one of the most important things I know: a cat knows how you feel before you say a word.

Twenty-five years have passed, and cats have never left my life. Today I care for the street cats in my neighborhood and the cats at our local shelter. I carry food, fill water bowls, look after the ones who fall sick, and slowly earn the trust of the shy ones.

On the days I am sad, they sit quietly beside me. On the days I am anxious, they give me a slow blink, as if to say “calm down.” I grew up in Istanbul, a city where cats belong to everyone, and I believe they carry a spiritual energy that comes to keep us company.
I set my own intention into every piece. They are not miracles. They are reminders to breathe, to slow down, and to remember you are not alone.
text.signature: With purrs, Mira & the Nine Lives

notes.p: These pieces are for reflection, comfort and inspiration. They are not a medical product, do not replace professional care, and no specific result is promised.

text.postsText: Cat legends from around the world, retold for the Nine Lives, and news from our small corner of Istanbul.
text.contactText: Want a guardian for a feeling we haven't painted yet? Have a question about printing, or something that didn't go right? Write to me. I read every message myself.
text.contactThanks: Thank you. Your message reached me, and I will reply by email as soon as I can.

products.name: Moonlight Cat
products.label: Guardian 1
products.intro: The first life a cat gives away. It keeps watch over your sleep.
products.story:
When a cat gives away its first life, that life does not disappear. It drifts up past the rooftops and settles on a lavender cloud under the Milky Way. That is where the Moonlight Cat sleeps, curled into a perfect circle, the full moon glowing above it.

It keeps watch over everyone who cannot rest. On the nights your thoughts keep turning, it comes to the edge of your dreams and breathes slowly, in and out, until you find yourself breathing with it. By the time you notice, the day has already let you go.
products.alt: Sleeping Tabby on a Moonlit Cloud

products.name: Healing Purr Cat
products.label: Guardian 2
products.intro: The second life. It sits with you on heavy days and purrs until you feel lighter.
products.story:
The second life became a tuxedo cat who sits on a golden cloud with its eyes half closed. A small heart of light glows in its chest, and every purr sends a soft ring of gold out into the pink sky.

You may have met this cat in real life. It is the cat who finds you on a hard day and climbs onto your lap without being asked. It does not fix anything. It simply stays, humming low and steady, until your shoulders drop and your breath slows down to match its own.
products.alt: Soothing Heart Light and Purr Waves on Golden Clouds

products.name: Nazar Guardian
products.label: Guardian 3
products.intro: The third life. It sits at the edge of your home with blue nazar lights circling around it.
products.story:
In Istanbul, a blue nazar bead hangs by almost every door, and a cat sits on almost every doorstep. The third life brought the two together.

The Nazar Guardian is a black cat with amber eyes, sitting calmly inside a ring of violet light far out in the galaxy. Blue nazar beads float around it like watchful eyes. It does not hiss and it does not chase. It just watches. Whatever is not meant for you drifts past and fades into the stars. Whatever belongs to you is allowed to stay.
products.alt: Evil Eye Protection Circle in a Galaxy

products.name: Golden Cat
products.label: Guardian 4
products.intro: The fourth life. Wherever its paws touch, gold ripples outward.
products.story:
The fourth life became an orange tabby who walks a river of liquid gold under a deep blue sky. It never hurries. Every step sends rings of light spreading out around its paws, and tiny sparks rise around it like fireflies.

Cats never feel guilty about taking the sunniest spot or the softest blanket. They accept good things as if they were always meant to have them. The Golden Cat walks with that same calm, and it asks you to try it too: receiving is a skill, and you are allowed to learn it.
products.alt: Orange Tabby Walking on Golden Light Ripples

products.name: Lucky Cat
products.label: Guardian 5
products.intro: The fifth life. Each time it steps forward, a new stone of light appears under its paw.
products.story:
The fifth life became a grey and white cat walking toward a door of light. The path is made of jade and gold stones, but there is a secret to it. The stones are not there until the cat steps. Each one appears only when a paw comes down.

That is how luck works for the Lucky Cat. It cannot see the whole road, and it does not wait until it can. It walks, and the road answers. It will not carry luck to your door, but it will walk beside you while you go and find it.
products.alt: Grey Tabby Walking Toward a Door of Light

products.name: Rose Cat
products.label: Guardian 6
products.intro: The sixth life. It reaches for love the way a cat reaches for sunlight.
products.story:
The sixth life became a fluffy white cat sitting on a rose-pink cloud. Above it hangs a heart made of pink light and stardust, and the cat looks up at it with wide amber eyes, without any doubt at all.

A cat lying in a patch of sun never asks whether it deserves the warmth. It just turns toward it and stays. The Rose Cat reaches for love in the same simple way. It reminds you that the first heart you are allowed to open is your own.
products.alt: Gazing Up at a Rose Heart Nebula

products.name: Karma Cat
products.label: Guardian 7
products.intro: The seventh life. It shakes old threads loose and lets the stars carry them away.
products.story:
The seventh life became a tortoiseshell cat standing on a slow cosmic spiral. Fine violet threads lift away from its fur, one by one, and drift off into the nebula until they turn into small golden sparks.

Watch a cat after a stressful moment. It shakes itself from nose to tail, licks a paw, and walks on as if nothing happened. It does not keep the moment. The Karma Cat does the same with old hurts and old habits. Letting go, it says, is not losing. It is making room.
products.alt: Tortoiseshell Releasing Violet Threads into the Stars

products.name: Third Eye Cat
products.label: Guardian 8
products.intro: The eighth life. It stares at an empty corner and knows something is there.
products.story:
Every cat person knows this moment. Your cat suddenly stares at an empty corner, ears forward, completely still. You see nothing. The cat is sure.

The eighth life became that kind of knowing. The Third Eye Cat is a Siamese sitting tall on a block of clear crystal, a small indigo light glowing on its forehead. It looks straight at you with calm blue eyes. It listens to quiet things, not loud ones, and it reminds you that your first soft feeling is often your truest one.
products.alt: Third Eye Light and Indigo Galaxy Rings

products.name: Phoenix Cat
products.label: Guardian 9
products.intro: The ninth and last life. Born from the moment a cat lands on its feet after a fall.
products.story:
The ninth life is the last one, and the bravest. It was born in the split second when a falling cat twists in the air and lands on its feet.

The Phoenix Cat is a ginger tabby leaping out of glowing embers into a pink and gold dawn, a long trail of fire-light streaming behind it like a comet. It carries nothing from the fall except the landing. It is for anyone starting over after a hard chapter, and it says the same thing every time: you can begin again as many times as you need.
products.alt: Ginger Tabby Leaping from Golden Embers at Dawn

products.name: Aura Cat
products.label: Spirit Companion
products.intro: Cats spend hours grooming, as if they know energy needs care too.
products.story:
After a busy day, a cat finds a quiet corner and begins to groom. Slowly, carefully, from ears to tail, until it looks like itself again.

The Aura Cat is a silver tabby with bright green eyes, sitting on a lake of starlight so still it looks like a mirror. Grey dust and smoky specks lift off its fur and scatter away. What is left is a soft rainbow glow of violet, mint and gold. It is the cat for the end of crowded days, a reminder that you are allowed to come back to yourself.
products.alt: Silver Tabby on a Starlit Lake

products.name: Amethyst Kitty
products.label: Spirit Companion
products.intro: Cats always find the quietest spot in a room. This one found the heart of an amethyst.
products.story:
Every cat knows where the warmest, quietest spot in a house is. It finds it within minutes and claims it.

The Amethyst Kitty went looking for the quietest place of all and found it inside a cluster of glowing amethyst, floating on violet clouds. It lies there with one paw resting on the crystal, eyes open, soft violet light on its chin. It is not asleep. It is calm and awake at the same time, and it shows you that peace can look like clear, steady attention.
products.alt: Cream Kitty Resting on Glowing Amethyst Crystals

products.name: Full Moon Kitty
products.label: Spirit Companion
products.intro: Every cat has stood up to reach for something just out of reach. This one reaches for the moon.
products.story:
You have seen it. A cat rises onto its back legs and stretches toward a toy on a shelf, a bird at the window, something just too high.

The Full Moon Kitty is a black and white cat doing exactly that, under an enormous glowing moon. Thin silver threads fall from the moon toward its paws. It does not sit and wait for a wish to drop into its lap. It stretches, it reaches, and the moon seems to lean a little closer. Its night is the full moon, when you name one wish and take one small step toward it.
products.alt: Tuxedo Kitty Reaching for the Full Moon

products.name: Starseed Cat
products.label: Spirit Companion
products.intro: Some cats stare at the night sky for a long time, as if remembering something.
products.story:
Some cats sit at the window long after dark, staring up at the sky without moving, as if they are remembering a place.

The Starseed Cat remembers. It is a Russian blue walking calmly along a winding road of golden stardust toward a glowing spiral galaxy. Every step leaves a little trail of light behind it. It is the cat for anyone who has ever felt a bit out of place, a quiet sign that there is a path, and that someone has already lit it for you.
products.alt: Russian Blue Walking a Golden Stardust Path

products.name: Crystal Shield Cat
products.label: Spirit Companion
products.intro: A cat always knows where its space ends and yours begins.
products.story:
A cat will happily sit beside you, but it will also tell you, very clearly, when it needs room. It never apologizes for that.

The Crystal Shield Cat carries that knowing as a sphere of shimmering crystal light. It sits calmly inside it, floating among soft blue clouds, while wisps of dark smoke outside bounce off and fade away. It is the cat for busy offices, crowded days and heavy rooms. It reminds you that boundaries are not walls. They are a kind of care.
products.alt: Grey Tabby Inside a Crystal Light Sphere

products.name: Golden Joy Kitty
products.label: Spirit Companion
products.intro: Cats never forget how to play, even when they are old.
products.story:
Even an old cat will suddenly chase a ray of light across the floor, as if it were a kitten again.

The Golden Joy Kitty is an orange and white cat leaping over golden morning clouds, both front paws reaching for floating bubbles of light. Every bubble it touches bursts into a tiny sun. It is the cat for kitchens, kids' rooms and grey mornings, and it carries one small message: lightness is not childish. It is a kind of strength.
products.alt: Orange and White Kitty Leaping for Bubbles of Light

products.name: Sunrise Cat
products.label: Spirit Companion
products.intro: A small cat will face down a big dog without blinking.
products.story:
On the streets of Istanbul you can see it often: a small cat standing its ground in front of a dog three times its size, calm and perfectly still.

The Sunrise Cat carries that courage to the top of a rocky peak. It climbs there before dawn, a ginger tabby standing above a sea of golden clouds, and greets the rising sun as an equal. Its shadow stretches long across the rock. It is the cat for new jobs, new homes and brave beginnings. Courage, it says, is not having no fear. It is standing tall anyway.
products.alt: Ginger Tabby on a Mountain Peak at Sunrise

posts.title: The Cat Who Talks You to Sleep
posts.excerpt: In old Russian tales, a great black cat named Bayun tells stories so soft that whoever hears them falls asleep. Catch him, and his stories become medicine.
posts.source: Retold from the Russian folk tale of Kot Bayun.
posts.body:
In the old fairy tales of Russia there is a cat called Bayun. His name comes from an old word for talking, and talking is what he does best. He sits high on an iron pole at the edge of a far-away land, and he tells stories. Endless stories, in a voice so warm and slow that it carries for miles.

Travellers who hear him start to yawn. Their steps get heavy. Before they know it, they are asleep on the road. In the oldest versions of the tale, that is where the danger lies: Bayun's sleep is so deep that some never wake.

But the tales also keep a secret. If you can stay awake while he talks, and if you are brave enough to reach him, the great cat changes. He stops being a danger and becomes your companion. From then on, his stories do the opposite of harm. They heal. People said that whoever had Bayun by their side would be kept from illness, because his voice could talk the pain out of a body.

I think about Bayun on nights when my mind will not stop. You know those nights. The day replays itself, the worries line up one by one, and sleep stays on the other side of the room.

That is when the cats come. One curls up against my legs, another settles on my chest, and they start to purr. Low and steady, like a story without words. I stop following my thoughts and start following the purr. And somewhere in the middle of it, I am asleep.

Maybe that is what the old storytellers understood. A cat's voice can pull you under, or it can carry you through. It depends on whether you fight it or let it hold you.

Our Healing Purr Cat was born from this feeling. Keep it near your bed, breathe slowly with it, and let it tell you the story your body needs tonight.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: The Learned Cat, the storytelling cat of Russian tales. Ivan Bilibin, 1910. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

gallery.caption: The storytelling cat walking along its golden chain around the great oak. Ivan Bilibin, 1905 (detail). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

posts.title: The Cat at the Gate
posts.excerpt: A traveller in old Japan saw a cat lift its paw at a gate, as if calling him in. He followed, and moments later the storm broke. This is where the beckoning cat began.
posts.source: Retold from the Japanese legend of the maneki-neko, the beckoning cat.
posts.body:
You have probably seen the little cat with one paw raised, waving from the counter of a shop. In Japan it is called maneki-neko, the beckoning cat. There are many stories about where it came from. This is the one I love most.

More than three hundred years ago, a lord named Ii Naotaka was riding home on a grey afternoon near what is now Tokyo. As he passed a quiet gate on the side of the road, he noticed a cat sitting there. It looked straight at him and lifted its paw, again and again, as if to say: come in, come here.

It was such a strange little gesture that he stopped. He got down from his horse and walked through the gate to look closer at the cat.

A moment later the sky opened. Thunder rolled over the road, and rain came down so hard that the path he had been riding on turned to mud. In some tellings, lightning struck the very place where he had just stood. He waited out the storm in shelter, dry and safe, with the cat beside him.

He never forgot that cat. The place became known for it, and over the years people began to make little figures of a cat with its paw raised, to call good fortune through their own doors.

What I love about this story is how small the moment is. No magic words, no miracle. Just a cat who noticed someone, and a person who was willing to stop and notice back.

I see it all the time with the street cats in my neighborhood. A cat waits by a door, looks at you, and somehow you change your route. Luck often starts like that: with paying attention.

Our Lucky Cat walks toward a door of light for this reason. Hang it where you start your day, and let it remind you to look up, slow down, and follow the small signs.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: A street seller with beckoning cat figures. Utagawa Hiroshige, Flourishing Business in Balladtown, 1852 (detail). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

gallery.caption: Thousands of beckoning cats left by visitors at Gōtoku-ji, Tokyo, the place where the legend is told. Photo: Niwrat, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

posts.title: The Cat Who Guarded the Home
posts.excerpt: In ancient Egypt, cats kept the grain safe and the house calm. They were so loved that a goddess with the face of a cat watched over every home.
posts.credit: Cat statuette, Egypt, Ptolemaic Period (332–30 BC). The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
posts.source: Retold from the ancient Egyptian traditions of Bastet and the household cat.
posts.body:
Long ago, along the river Nile, every family stored its grain in clay jars. Mice came for the grain, and snakes came for the mice. Then the cats came, and the house grew quiet again.

The Egyptians noticed. A cat asked for very little: a warm step in the sun, a bowl of milk, a place by the door. In return it guarded everything that kept a family alive. Slowly the cat became more than a helper. It became a sign of home itself.

They gave that feeling a name and a face. Bastet was the goddess of the home, of joy, music and protection, and she was shown with the head of a cat. In her city, people held festivals with singing and dancing in her honour. In ordinary houses, the family cat was treated like a small part of her, sitting at the edge of the room and keeping watch.

An old Greek traveller wrote that when a cat died in an Egyptian home, the whole family shaved their eyebrows in mourning. Whether every family did this or not, the story tells you how much a cat could mean.

I understand them. In Istanbul, cats sit on doorsteps all over the city, and it often feels as if each one has chosen a house to look after. They are not loud guards. They simply stay, and their calm settles over the place like a blanket.

Our Nazar Guardian carries that ancient job. Hang it near your door, and let it sit at the edge of your home the way cats have done for thousands of years.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: The Goddess Who Rode With Cats
posts.excerpt: In Norse myth, Freyja, the goddess of love, did not ride horses. Her chariot was pulled by two great cats across the sky.
posts.credit: Freyja in her chariot drawn by cats. Emil Doepler, around 1905. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
posts.source: Retold from the Norse myths of Freyja, as written down in the Prose Edda.
posts.body:
In the old stories of the North, the gods travelled in grand ways. Thor rode in a chariot pulled by goats, and Odin rode an eight-legged horse. But Freyja, the goddess of love and beauty, chose something different. Her chariot was pulled by two large cats.

The old texts do not say much more than that, and maybe they do not need to. Imagine it: a goddess crossing the sky, and in front of her two cats running through the clouds, their tails high, their paws hardly touching the wind.

Why cats? Nobody knows for sure. Some say it is because cats are soft and fierce at the same time, just like love. A cat can curl up on your lap and purr, and a moment later it can turn and walk away, because it decides for itself where it belongs. Love that is real has that same freedom in it.

People in the North say that farmers once left small gifts out for Freyja's cats, hoping for a good harvest and a happy home. The cats were her messengers, and kindness to a cat was kindness to her.

I like to think that every cat still carries a little of that chariot in its step. Watch a cat run across a garden at dusk and tell me it does not look like it is pulling something invisible behind it.

Our Rose Cat reaches for love the way Freyja's cats ran: freely, and without asking permission. Keep it near you as a reminder that love begins with being gentle with yourself.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: The Boy Who Drew Cats
posts.excerpt: A Japanese boy could not stop drawing cats. One stormy night, in an empty building far from home, his drawings came to life to protect him.
posts.credit: Cover of The Boy Who Drew Cats, retold by Lafcadio Hearn. Illustration by Suzuki Kason, 1898. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

gallery.caption: The boy at his desk, from the 1898 edition. Illustration by Suzuki Kason. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

posts.source: Retold from the Japanese folk tale The Boy Who Drew Cats, published in English by Lafcadio Hearn in 1898.
posts.body:
Long ago in Japan, a farmer had a son who was small and gentle and not strong enough for work in the fields. So the family sent him to study with an old teacher, hoping he would become a scholar.

The boy was clever and kind, but he had one habit he could not break. He drew cats. He drew them in the margins of his books, on the walls, on the paper screens, everywhere. Sleeping cats, stretching cats, cats watching the door. His teacher sighed and finally told him: You will never be a scholar. Perhaps you will be an artist. But remember one thing. At night, avoid large places. Keep to small ones.

The boy walked away with his small bundle and his brushes. When night fell, he found a large empty building on a hill and went inside to rest. He did not know that a terrible creature lived there, a giant rat that frightened every traveller away.

The building had big white screens, and the boy could not help himself. He took out his brush and covered them with cats. Then, tired, he remembered his teacher's words, crawled into a small cabinet and fell asleep.

In the night he woke to a huge noise of fighting and screeching. He stayed very still in his small hiding place until it was quiet. In the morning he crept out. The giant rat was gone for good. And on the screens, every cat he had drawn had moved a little, as if they had all come down to fight for him and then climbed back into the paper.

The boy grew up to be a famous painter of cats, and people say some of his cats can still be seen today.

I love this story because the boy did not win by being strong. He won by doing the thing he loved, and by listening to good advice. Our Crystal Shield Cat keeps that same promise: a quiet circle of protection around the one who made it.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: Dick Whittington and His Cat
posts.excerpt: A poor boy in old London owned nothing but a cat. That cat sailed across the sea and came back with a fortune.
posts.credit: Whittington and his cat, from The History of Sir Richard Whittington, printed in Boston, 1770 (detail). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
posts.source: Retold from the English folk tale of Dick Whittington and his cat.
posts.body:
There once was a poor boy called Dick who walked all the way to London, because he had heard that its streets were paved with gold. They were not. He found cold stones, hungry nights and a kitchen job in a merchant's house, where he slept in an attic full of rats.

With the only penny he had, Dick bought a cat. From that night on, the rats left him alone, and he finally slept.

One day the merchant prepared a ship for a long voyage. He told everyone in the house that they could send something along to sell, and share in the profit. Dick had only one thing in the world. With a heavy heart, he sent his cat.

The ship sailed far away to a rich kingdom whose palace was overrun by rats and mice. They ran across the tables at every feast. When the ship's captain set Dick's cat down in the royal dining hall, it cleared the room in minutes. The king was so delighted that he paid more for the cat than for everything else on the ship together.

Back in London, Dick had become so unhappy that he packed his bundle and ran away. As he sat resting on a hill outside the city, the church bells began to ring, and they seemed to say: Turn again, Whittington, Lord Mayor of London. So he turned back. Soon the ship came home with his fortune, and in time he really did become Lord Mayor.

There was a real Richard Whittington who was Mayor of London four times, six hundred years ago. Whether he had a cat, nobody knows. But people have told his story with a cat in it for centuries, because they understood something true: sometimes the smallest thing you have is the one that changes everything.

Our Golden Cat walks a river of light for that reason. Keep it where you plan your days, as a reminder that good things often start very small.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: The King of the Cats
posts.excerpt: A man walking home at night saw nine black cats carrying a tiny crown. When he told the story at home, his own cat had something to say about it.
posts.credit: Illustration by John D. Batten for More English Fairy Tales, 1894. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
posts.source: Retold from the English and Irish folk tale The King of the Cats, as collected by Joseph Jacobs in 1894.
posts.body:
One winter evening, a man came home late and sat by the fire, looking very strange. His wife was knitting, and their old black cat, Tom, was asleep on the hearth.

You will never believe what I saw tonight, the man said. I was walking past the old church, and I saw nine black cats walking in a slow line. Each had a white spot on its chest. They were carrying something small between them, covered with a black cloth, and on top of it was a tiny golden crown. And every three steps they all cried together: Miaou!

As he spoke, old Tom lifted his head and looked at him.

Then, the man went on, the cats came toward me and the one in front looked straight at me and said, in a clear voice: Tell Tom Tildrum that Tim Toldrum is dead.

Who could Tom Tildrum be? asked his wife.

But before he could answer, old Tom leapt up from the hearth, his eyes shining. What? he cried. Old Tim is dead? Then I am the King of the Cats! And with that he shot up the chimney and was never seen in that house again.

This story has been told in England and Ireland for a very long time, and I think every cat person secretly believes it. Look at your cat sleeping by the radiator. Are you sure you know everything about where it goes at night? Are you sure it is not royalty somewhere?

Cats have always seemed to live in two worlds at once: ours, and another one we only catch glimpses of. Our Third Eye Cat sits right on that border, watching the things we cannot see.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: The Fairy Cat of the Highlands
posts.excerpt: In the Scottish Highlands, people told of a large black fairy cat with a white star on its chest. On one autumn night, a saucer of milk could earn its blessing.
posts.credit: Black cat, from Cats: Pictures Without Words. Théophile Steinlen, around 1898. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
posts.source: Retold from the Scottish and Irish folklore of the Cat Sìth.
posts.body:
In the misty hills of Scotland, people used to speak quietly about a creature called the Cat Sìth, the fairy cat. It was said to be as large as a dog, black from nose to tail, except for one white mark on its chest, like a small star.

The Cat Sìth was not an ordinary animal. It belonged to the fairy folk, and it walked between their world and ours whenever it pleased.

On Samhain, the old autumn festival at the end of October, the border between the two worlds was believed to grow thin. On that night, families would set a saucer of fresh milk outside the door before going to bed. If the Cat Sìth passed by and drank from it, the house would be blessed for the whole coming year. Homes that forgot were said to find their cows giving less milk all winter.

The old tales have darker parts too, as fairy tales often do. But the custom I love is the simplest one: on the coldest night of the season, people left something warm and good out for a cat they could not see, just in case it came.

We still do this in our own way. Every night in my neighborhood, someone leaves food and water out for the street cats. Most of the time we never see who comes to eat it. In the morning the bowls are empty, and somehow the street feels a little kinder.

This story belongs with our Moonlight Cat, who keeps watch in the dark while you sleep. Maybe on the last night of October, leave a little light on for it.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: The Book of Lucky Cats
posts.excerpt: In old Siam, scholars wrote poems about cats and painted them in folding books. Each cat had its own colours, its own markings and its own kind of luck.
posts.credit: Pages from a Thai treatise on cats (Tamra Maew), 19th century. British Library, Or. 16797. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
posts.source: Retold from the Thai tradition of the Tamra Maew, the Treatise on Cats.
posts.body:
In the old kingdom of Siam, now Thailand, there was a special kind of book. It was made of long strips of paper folded like an accordion, and on its pages, painted by hand, were cats. Next to each cat was a short poem.

These books were called Tamra Maew, the Treatise on Cats. Their poems are believed to go back hundreds of years, to the time of the old capital Ayutthaya. Copies were made again and again, by hand, so that the knowledge would not be lost.

Each page described one kind of cat: the colour of its coat, the shape of its markings, the colour of its eyes. And each cat brought its own kind of good fortune to the home that cared for it. One silver-blue cat was said to bring luck and prosperity. A pure white cat with bright eyes was called a white jewel. A cat with dark points on its face, ears, paws and tail, very much like the cat we now call the Siamese, was one of the most treasured of all.

The books also listed a few cats that were said to bring bad luck. I prefer to leave those pages closed. Every cat I have known has brought something good, even the grumpy ones.

What moves me about these books is the care in them. Someone sat for hours painting the exact curve of a tail and the exact colour of an eye, because they believed each cat was worth remembering.

Our Lucky Cat walks a road of jade and gold for this reason. Hang it where you begin your day, and let it remind you that luck often arrives in the shape of a cat.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: Why Willows Grow Kittens
posts.excerpt: In Poland they say the soft grey buds of the willow tree are tiny kittens. The reason is a story about a crying mother cat and a kind tree.
posts.credit: Pussy willow branches in spring. Photo: W.carter, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
posts.source: Retold from a Polish folk legend about the pussy willow.
posts.body:
In early spring, before the leaves come, willow branches in many parts of the world grow small, soft, silver-grey buds. Touch one and it feels exactly like fur. In English they are called pussy willows. In Polish they are called kotki, which means little kittens. There is a story behind that name.

Long ago, a mother cat had a litter of kittens near a river. One warm day the kittens were chasing butterflies along the bank. They jumped and tumbled and played, and one by one they slipped into the cold, fast water.

The mother cat ran up and down the bank, crying for help. She could not swim against the current. Her kittens were being carried away.

The willow trees along the river heard her. They could not walk and they could not run, but they could bend. They lowered their long branches into the water, and the kittens caught hold with their little claws. Slowly, the willows lifted them back to the bank, wet and shivering but safe, into their mother's arms.

Ever since that day, people say, the willows remember. Every spring, their branches grow soft grey buds, as soft as kitten fur, in honour of the little ones they saved.

In many homes, willow branches are still brought inside in spring as a sign that winter is over and life is starting again.

This is a story of rescue and of new beginnings, and it belongs with our Phoenix Cat. Whenever you have been carried too far by the current, remember the willows. Something will bend down to help you back to the bank.

With purrs,
Mira

posts.title: The Cat Who Kept a Baby Warm
posts.excerpt: On a freezing January night in Russia, a street cat climbed into a cardboard box beside an abandoned baby and refused to leave until help came.
posts.source: Based on real events reported in Russia in January 2015. Names have been changed.
posts.body:
In a small town near Moscow, the neighbours shared a cat. She was a long-haired tabby, and everyone on the street knew her. We will call her Lyra. She slept in stairwells, ate from bowls that kind people left out, and belonged to all of them a little.

One January night, the temperature fell far below zero. Someone had left a cardboard box on the ground near the apartment buildings. Inside, wrapped in a blanket, was a baby boy only a few months old.

Lyra found him before any person did. She climbed into the box, curled her warm body against the baby, and stayed there. And she did something else. She began to cry out, loudly and without stopping, until a woman passing by, whom we will call Galina, came to see what was wrong.

Galina later told reporters that the cat was lying right next to the child, keeping him warm, and that she had been meowing to call for help. When the ambulance came, Lyra followed the medics all the way to the vehicle, still crying, as if she wanted to be sure the baby was safe.

The doctors said the boy was healthy. He had been outside for a few hours, and the cat's warmth had helped protect him from the cold.

I read this story many years ago and I still think about it. A street cat, who owned nothing, gave the only thing she had: her warmth, and her voice.

This is why our Healing Purr Cat sits with a glowing heart in its chest. Some comfort cannot be explained. It just stays beside you until help arrives.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: Illustration made for Nine Lives Spirit Cats.

posts.title: The Cat Who Saved a Railway
posts.excerpt: A small country railway in Japan was about to close. Then a calico cat was named stationmaster, and people came from all over the world to meet her.
posts.source: Based on the real story of a station cat in Wakayama, Japan, from 2007 to 2015. Names have been changed.
posts.body:
In the countryside of southern Japan, there was a little railway line that ran between rice fields and quiet villages. For years, fewer and fewer people rode it. The company was losing money, and the line was going to be closed.

At one small station on that line lived a calico cat. We will call her Hoshi, which means star. She had grown up near the station shop, and the local people loved her. When the railway decided that the station would no longer have human staff, someone had an unusual idea. Why not make Hoshi the stationmaster?

So in 2007, a calico cat officially became the head of a train station. She sat at the gate every day and greeted the passengers, calm and dignified, the way only a cat can be.

People were charmed. They came to visit her, first from nearby towns, then from all over Japan, then from other countries. Ridership grew. Special trains were painted in her honour. One study estimated that in her first year she brought millions of dollars of visitors into the local economy. The little line that was about to disappear stayed open.

Hoshi kept her job for the rest of her life. When she passed away in 2015, thousands of people came to say goodbye, and another calico cat took over her post.

I love this story because nobody planned it. A cat simply sat where she always sat, and her quiet presence turned a forgotten place into somewhere people wanted to be.

Our Lucky Cat walks toward an open door of light. Sometimes luck arrives exactly like this: a cat at the gate, and a road that does not close after all.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: Illustration made for Nine Lives Spirit Cats.

posts.title: The Cat Who Would Not Let Her Sleep
posts.excerpt: A woman adopted a big orange cat from a shelter. That very night, he woke her son and saved her life.
posts.source: Based on real events reported in Wisconsin, USA, in 2012. Names have been changed.
posts.body:
One winter afternoon in the United States, a woman we will call Claire went to an animal shelter with her teenage son, Oliver. They only meant to look. But they met a huge orange and white cat, more than nine kilograms of fur, sitting next to his best friend, a smaller cat. We will call them Marmalade and Pip. Claire could not leave them behind, so she took both of them home that same day.

Claire had lived with diabetes since she was a child. That night, while she was asleep, her blood sugar dropped dangerously low and she began to have a seizure.

Marmalade had been in the house for only a few hours. He did not know the rooms yet, and he did not know these people. But he knew something was wrong. He climbed onto Claire's chest and pushed at her face, nudging and nipping, trying to wake her. She came to just enough to call out for her son, but Oliver did not hear her.

So Marmalade ran down the hall into Oliver's room and jumped on his bed again and again until the boy woke up. Oliver ran to his mother and called for help, and she received treatment in time.

Claire and her doctors believed that without the cat, she might not have survived the night. Later, Marmalade learned to sit at her feet and meow when he sensed her blood sugar was low.

When people ask me why I believe cats notice everything, I tell them stories like this one. A cat who had known her for a few hours already understood that she was his to look after.

Our Moonlight Cat keeps watch while you sleep. This is the real-life version.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: Illustration made for Nine Lives Spirit Cats.

posts.title: The Mother Who Walked Into the Fire
posts.excerpt: When an old garage caught fire in New York, a stray mother cat went back into the flames again and again, until all five of her kittens were outside.
posts.source: Based on real events in Brooklyn, New York, in March 1996. Names have been changed.
posts.body:
On a spring morning in Brooklyn, New York, firefighters were called to an abandoned garage that was burning. As they worked to bring the flames under control, one of them, whom we will call Michael, noticed something strange.

A stray cat was coming out of the burning building with a tiny kitten in her mouth. She set it down on the pavement across the street. Then she turned around and went back inside.

She did it again. And again. Five times she walked into the smoke and heat, and five times she came back out carrying one of her kittens. We will call her Ember.

By the end, Ember was badly hurt. Her eyes were blistered shut, her ears and paws were burned, and much of her fur was gone. She could not see her kittens anymore. So she went to each one and touched it gently with her nose, one by one, as if counting them. Only when she knew all five were there did she collapse.

Michael wrapped the family up and took them to an animal hospital. The doctors cared for them for months. Ember slowly recovered, and four of her kittens grew strong. One small white kitten became sick a month later and did not survive.

Ember's story travelled around the world. Thousands of people wrote letters asking to adopt her. In the end, she went to a loving home where she lived a long, quiet life.

I have watched many street mothers in my neighborhood move their kittens one by one to a safer corner. Ember did the same thing, only through fire.

Our Phoenix Cat rises out of the embers. Every time I look at it, I think of her.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: Illustration made for Nine Lives Spirit Cats.

posts.title: The Cat Who Stayed
posts.excerpt: In a care home in New England, one grey and white cat seemed to know when a resident needed company most, and he would not leave their side.
posts.source: Based on the real story of a care home cat in Rhode Island, USA, first described by his doctor in 2007. Names have been changed.
posts.body:
In a care home in New England lived a grey and white cat. We will call him Milo. He had grown up there since he was a kitten. Most of the residents were very old and very ill, and many of them no longer recognised the people around them.

Milo was not especially friendly. He did his rounds of the hallways like a nurse, looked into rooms, and moved on. But the staff began to notice a pattern. Every so often, Milo would walk into a room, jump onto the bed and curl up beside a resident. And he would stay there, purring quietly, for hours.

The residents he chose were always the ones who were close to the end of their lives.

A doctor at the home, whom we will call Dr. Bennett, wrote about Milo in a well-known medical journal. Over the years, the cat had kept company with many people in their final hours. The staff came to trust him so much that when Milo settled on someone's bed, they would call the family, so that they could come and say goodbye.

Nobody knows for sure how Milo knew. Perhaps he could smell small changes in the body. Perhaps he noticed how still a person became. What everyone agreed on was this: he did not want them to be alone.

This is a gentle story, and a sad one. But when I read it, I mostly feel comfort. The cats I have cared for over the years have always found me on my hardest days and sat with me without asking for anything. Milo did that for strangers, at the most important moment of all.

Our Healing Purr Cat is for those moments. It does not fix the sadness. It stays.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: Illustration made for Nine Lives Spirit Cats.

posts.title: The Ship's Cat
posts.excerpt: A young sailor found a skinny kitten at a harbour in Hong Kong. A year later, that cat was wounded in battle, kept the crew's spirits up, and received a medal for bravery.
posts.source: Based on the real story of a Royal Navy ship's cat in China in 1949. Names have been changed.
posts.body:
In 1948, at the docks of Hong Kong, a seventeen-year-old sailor we will call Thomas found a thin black and white kitten wandering alone. He hid it in his jacket and carried it aboard his ship. We will call the cat Barnaby.

Barnaby quickly made himself at home. He caught rats, slept in the captain's cap, and became everyone's friend.

In the spring of 1949, the ship was sailing up a great river in China when it came under heavy fire. Many sailors were hurt, and the captain was killed. Barnaby was badly wounded too. Frightened, he hid deep in the bottom of the ship for days. When hunger finally brought him out, the crew found him with four wounds and took him to the ship's doctor, who treated him.

The ship could not escape. For almost ten weeks it was trapped in the middle of the river, with little food and hot summer days. Rats spread through the ship and threatened the supplies. As soon as he could walk, Barnaby went back to work and kept them away. And he did one more important thing. He visited the injured sailors in the sick bay and lay beside them. The crew said he lifted their spirits when they needed it most.

When the ship finally escaped and sailed home, Barnaby became famous. He was awarded a medal for animal bravery, the first cat ever to receive it. Sadly, he became ill soon after arriving in England and died that same year. He was buried with full honours.

Courage does not always look like a lion. Sometimes it looks like a small, wounded cat going back to work, and lying beside a frightened young sailor at night.

Our Sunrise Cat stands tall on its rock for this reason. Courage is not having no fear. It is standing up anyway.

With purrs,
Mira
posts.credit: Illustration made for Nine Lives Spirit Cats.
